prior_terminal_row.title: Council for National Policy List Compiles More Than 1,000 Names
prior_terminal_row.description_short: Council for National Policy List Compiles More Than 1,000 Names
prior_terminal_row.description_medium: The Council for National Policy formed in 1981 as a private forum for conservative organizers, donors and activists. A later Trump Timeline page compiled 1,011 names from 1981 to 2020 and acknowledged that the list might include fewer than half of the council’s members. The compilation does not establish that Donald Trump belonged to the group.
prior_terminal_row.description_long: The Council for National Policy began in 1981 as a private forum for conservative organizers, donors and activists. A contemporaneous New York Times report described more than 50 conservatives gathering to form an umbrella organization they hoped would gain influence. Decades later, a Trump Timeline page published a list of 1,011 names spanning 1981 through 2020 and acknowledged that it might include fewer than half of the council’s members. Because the compilation is incomplete and covers many years, it does not show when a person joined or what role that person played. The synopsis names figures such as Charlie Kirk and Kellyanne Conway, but does not establish Donald Trump’s membership or participation. Nor does the list tie the council’s activity to a specific Trump policy or campaign action. A partial name list alone cannot establish influence over a policy or coordination with a president.

title: Donald Trump sues the U.S. government for discrimination

prior_terminal_row.title: Donald Trump sues the U.S. government for discrimination
prior_terminal_row.description_short: Donald Trump sues the U.S. government for discrimination
prior_terminal_row.description_medium: In 1993, Donald Trump sued the federal government over the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, arguing that the law favored tribal casinos and disadvantaged casino owners such as himself. The supplied account says he also challenged the law on states’ rights grounds and sought to block tribal casinos. It does not provide the court’s decision or the case’s later procedural history.
prior_terminal_row.description_long: Donald Trump filed a federal lawsuit in 1993 challenging the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, the 1988 law governing tribal gaming. As summarized in the supplied account, Trump argued that the law discriminated against him as a casino owner by allowing Native American tribes to open casinos, and he also claimed it infringed states’ rights. The New York Times headline linked to the record says the suit sought to block Indian casinos. These are arguments attributed to Trump’s complaint, not a judicial finding that the statute discriminated against him or violated states’ rights. The record does not identify the specific tribal parties, lay out the complete legal arguments, or show how the court resolved the dispute. Its linked Times report returned HTTP 403 in a focused read, and the supplied draft contained no ruling or docket details. The filing can be described as a challenge to tribal gaming under federal law, but the outcome and the court’s reasoning remain unknown from the available material. A fuller account needs the complaint or docket and a reliable source on the procedural disposition before it can say whether the suit was dismissed, decided on the merits or otherwise concluded.

title: Evercore Acquires American Media; David Pecker Becomes CEO

prior_terminal_row.title: Evercore Acquires American Media; David Pecker Becomes CEO
prior_terminal_row.description_short: Evercore Acquires American Media; David Pecker Becomes CEO
prior_terminal_row.description_medium: On February 17, 1999, Evercore Partners acquired American Media, publisher of the National Enquirer and Star, and David Pecker became the company’s chairman and CEO. This was a change in ownership at the parent company, not a personal purchase of the Enquirer by Pecker. The transaction does not establish the paper’s earlier Mafia financing claims.
prior_terminal_row.description_long: On February 17, 1999, Evercore Partners acquired American Media Inc., the publisher of the National Enquirer and Star. Evercore was led by Roger Altman, and David Pecker, then an executive at Hachette Filipacchi, was hired to lead American Media as chairman and chief executive. The transaction changed control of the parent publisher and put Pecker in charge of its publications; it was not a personal purchase of the Enquirer by Pecker. The distinction matters because the title describes a different buyer and a separate claim about the paper’s earlier history. This transaction record does not establish whether the National Enquirer had previously received Mafia financing, and the 1999 acquisition itself is not reported as involving Donald Trump. Pecker’s later relationship with Trump should not be projected backward onto the purchase. The reported event is Evercore’s acquisition of American Media and Pecker’s appointment to run the company.

title: Supreme Court Allows Hobby Lobby RFRA Claim Over Contraceptive Coverage

prior_terminal_row.title: Supreme Court Allows Hobby Lobby RFRA Claim Over Contraceptive Coverage
prior_terminal_row.description_short: Supreme Court Allows Hobby Lobby RFRA Claim Over Contraceptive Coverage
prior_terminal_row.description_medium: TrumpFile’s page presents the Supreme Court’s 2014 Burwell v. Hobby Lobby decision as granting corporations religious-freedom protections and compares those protections to individual rights. The case-specific account supplied for this record concerns closely held companies seeking a Religious Freedom Restoration Act exemption from the contraceptive-coverage rule. The TrumpFile page does not identify a Trump statement or action connected to the decision.
prior_terminal_row.description_long: TrumpFile’s timeline entry, dated June 30, 2014, reports the Supreme Court’s decision in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby and characterizes it as recognizing corporate religious-freedom protections. The page goes further, asserting that corporations consequently have the same rights as natural persons and might have more rights than individuals. The case-specific account supplied with this record describes a narrower holding: closely held for-profit corporations could bring a claim under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act against the Affordable Care Act’s contraceptive-coverage requirement. That is not a general declaration that corporations possess every human right. The difference matters because the page’s headline and argument broaden a defined statutory ruling. The linked TrumpFile entry identifies the 2014 case but does not document a Trump statement, appointment, policy, or other action tying him to the decision. The material supports describing the page’s characterization and the narrower legal issue, but it does not establish a Trump-specific event. A source connecting Trump to the ruling or documenting the statement attributed to him is still needed.

title: Trump Opens Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to Oil Drilling

prior_terminal_row.title: Trump Opens Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to Oil Drilling
prior_terminal_row.description_short: Trump Opens Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to Oil Drilling
prior_terminal_row.description_medium: In 2017, the Trump administration moved to open the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR) to oil and gas drilling, reversing decades of bipartisan conservation policy protecting one of America's last pristine wilderness areas. The refuge is home to polar bears, caribou, migratory birds, and the indigenous Gwich'in people who depend on its ecosystem. Environmental groups and scientists warned that drilling could cause irreversible damage to this fragile Arctic ecosystem. The move was seen as a major giveaway to the oil industry that had lobbied to access ANWR for years.
